summary: Streptokinase is a fibrinolytic protein derived from beta-hemolytic streptococci. It forms a complex with plasminogen that converts plasminogen to plasmin, dissolving fibrin clots. It is used (where available) for acute myocardial infarction, massive/submassive pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, arterial thrombosis/embolism, and occluded catheters. Major hazards are bleeding (including intracranial hemorrhage) and allergic/anaphylactic reactions; because it is antigenic, repeat use is limited.
indications: Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (lysis of coronary thrombi, where primary PCI is unavailable)
Acute massive or submassive pulmonary embolism
Clearance of occluded arteriovenous cannulae/central venous catheters

dosage.d: 1.5 million IU intravenously over 30 to 60 minutes
dosage.n: Start as early as possible, within 6 (ideally <12) hours of symptom onset

dosage.d: Loading 250,000 IU IV over 30 minutes, then 100,000 IU/hour
Loading 250,000 IU IV over 30 minutes, then 100,000 IU/hour
dosage.n: Continue maintenance infusion for up to 72 hours

dosage.d: Loading 250,000 IU over 30 minutes, then 100,000 IU/hour
dosage.n: Continue 24-72 hours per response; may use intra-arterial route

admin: Administer intravenously (or intra-arterially/intracoronary per protocol); the loading dose neutralizes circulating anti-streptokinase antibodies
Have resuscitation equipment, corticosteroids/antihistamines, and antifibrinolytics (e.g., aminocaproic/tranexamic acid) available
Avoid intramuscular injections and arterial punctures/invasive procedures during therapy; minimize venepunctures
Monitor for hypotension during infusion - slow or interrupt the infusion if marked hypotension occurs
Do NOT re-administer between 5 days and 12 months (or longer) after prior streptokinase or recent streptococcal infection due to neutralizing antibodies and allergy risk
moa: Streptokinase is a non-enzymatic protein from beta-hemolytic streptococci that binds circulating plasminogen to form an activator complex. This complex cleaves other plasminogen molecules to plasmin, a proteolytic enzyme that degrades fibrin (and fibrinogen), dissolving thrombi. It produces a systemic lytic (fibrinogenolytic) state, which underlies its bleeding risk.

absolute: History of hemorrhagic stroke or any stroke/CNS event within the recent period
Recent (e.g., within 2 months) intracranial or intraspinal surgery or trauma
Intracranial neoplasm, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm
Known bleeding diathesis / severe uncontrolled hypertension
Prior severe allergic reaction to streptokinase or anistreplase
relative: Recent major surgery, organ biopsy, or trauma (within ~10 days)
Recent GI/GU bleeding or active peptic ulcer
Recent prior streptokinase exposure or streptococcal infection (5 days to 12 months) - antibodies reduce efficacy and raise allergy risk
Pregnancy (especially first 18 weeks) and early postpartum
Advanced age, severe hepatic or renal disease, diabetic hemorrhagic retinopathy
monitor: ECG and reperfusion arrhythmias / coagulation parameters

preg: There are limited human data. Because of the high risk of maternal hemorrhage (including at the placental site), streptokinase should be used in pregnancy only when the potential benefit clearly outweighs the risk; it is generally avoided in the first 18 weeks and around delivery. As a large protein, placental transfer is expected to be limited, but bleeding risk to mother and fetus predominates.
lact: It is not known whether streptokinase is excreted in human milk; as a large protein, significant transfer into milk is unlikely. Use with caution; in the acute critical setting, breastfeeding is usually a secondary consideration.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required for renal impairment; however, comorbid bleeding risk should be assessed.
hepatic: Severe hepatic disease may cause coagulopathy and increase the risk of bleeding; use with caution.

major: Anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, DOACs) - markedly increased bleeding risk (though heparin is often used adjunctively under monitoring)
Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel, GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors) - increased bleeding risk
moderate: Drugs affecting platelet function (NSAIDs, dipyridamole) - increased bleeding
ACE inhibitors - may increase the risk of hypotension/anaphylactoid reactions during infusion
minor: Antifibrinolytic agents (aminocaproic acid, tranexamic acid) - antagonize the lytic effect (used as antidote for bleeding)
interactions.alcohol: Not directly relevant in the acute setting
interactions.diagnostics: Markedly prolongs thrombin time/PT/aPTT and lowers fibrinogen; reduces plasminogen and raises fibrin degradation products

common: Bleeding (oozing at puncture sites, ecchymosis, hematoma)
rare: Serum sickness, vasculitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome (delayed immune reactions)

monitoring: Continuous observation for bleeding, especially neurologic signs of intracranial hemorrhage
Blood pressure and heart rate during and after infusion
ECG and cardiac rhythm (reperfusion); markers of reperfusion success
counsel: This is an emergency clot-dissolving medicine given in hospital; tell staff immediately about any bleeding, severe headache, or weakness
Report any rash, itching, difficulty breathing, or feeling faint during the infusion (allergic reaction)
You may bruise or bleed more easily for a period afterward; avoid injury
Inform future doctors that you have received streptokinase - it usually should not be given again for a long time
After treatment you may be continued on anticoagulants/antiplatelets and will need monitoring
pk: Fibrinolysis begins within minutes of the infusion starting
Peak fibrinolytic effect during/shortly after the infusion
Biphasic; the active complex half-life is approximately 18 to 23 minutes (systemic lytic state persists longer)
Systemic fibrinolytic effect and reduced fibrinogen persist for several hours after the infusion
Store lyophilized powder refrigerated/at controlled room temperature per product label; reconstitute gently and use promptly
pearls: BLEEDING is the principal danger - intracranial hemorrhage is the most feared complication; have antifibrinolytics ready and avoid invasive procedures

ANTIGENIC: do not re-administer from ~5 days to 12 months after prior streptokinase or recent streptococcal infection - neutralizing antibodies reduce efficacy and increase anaphylaxis risk; use a fibrin-specific agent (alteplase/tenecteplase) instead
No longer marketed in the United States (withdrawn); data here reflect WHO/EMA/BNF and international labeling - fibrin-specific agents are preferred where available
Hypotension during infusion is common - slow the rate; reperfusion arrhythmias may occur in acute MI
missed: Not applicable - streptokinase is given as a one-time, monitored infusion in an emergency/critical-care setting, not on a self-administered schedule.
overdose: Overdose increases the risk of serious hemorrhage. Management: stop the infusion; replace clotting factors with fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen; reverse the lytic state with an antifibrinolytic agent (aminocaproic acid or tranexamic acid); transfuse as needed and provide supportive care. Treat anaphylaxis with epinephrine, antihistamines, and corticosteroids.
